newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden agrees on phase out plan for nuclear power.
newsitem.headline: Sweden agrees on phase out plan for nuclear power.

text.p: Sweden's ruling Social Democrat party on Monday gained support to phase out nuclear power, ending a 17-year-old deadlock.
"The Centre Party, the Left Party and the Social Demcorats have agreed on a proposal for an energy agreement," said Peter Akinder, spokesman for Swedish Energy Minister Anders Sundstrom.
These parties hold 210 of 349 seats in Sweden's parliament.
Swedish radio said the parties agreed to close one reactor at Barseback nuclear power plant before general elections in 1998 and a second after.
Negotiations are set to begin with the plant's owner, Swedish power company Sydkraft AB, about replacing the power source with either natural gas or oil, the radio said.

Denmark's Environment Minister Svend Auken welcomed a possible closure of Barseback, which is located within sight of Copenhagen and long a subject of dispute between the two normally placid Nordic neighbours.
The parties declined to confirm details about which reactors or how many would be targeted, saying they would inform their party groups in parliament on Tuesday.

"It is a very good and responsible agreement," Sundstrom said. "It concerns how a nuclear power phase out will begin and it meets demands that the industry will not be hurt. It will give increased employment."

A plan to phase out the country's nuclear programme has been in the air since a national referendum in 1980 when Swedes voted to gradually phase out nuclear power. Parliament eventually set 2010 as the target for making Sweden nuclear-free.
Critics of the plan say Sweden has not made alternative arrangements for electricity supply.

A proposal to replace the two reactors with natural gas or oil could go against a 1993 parliamentary ruling that in the year 2000 carbon dioxide emissions should not exceed 1990 levels and that they should decline after 2000.

Substitution with oil and gas does not seem to satisfy Sydkraft, which on Monday reiterated its demand for full compensation with "the same quantity of electricity production at current costs and environmental effects."
Nuclear power is cheaper and cleaner than oil or gas.
The government and its informal cooperation partner the Centre Party have previously said that nuclear power will be replaced by environmentally sustainable energy sources.
Critics say that such alternatives are too expensive for the electricity intensive industries, such as steel and forestry, which rely on cheap nuclear and hydro-electric power.
Sundstrom has previously attempted to postpone the closure of the first reactor until 2001 because of concern for industry and in order to buy time needed to find alternatives.

Nuclear power meets half of the country's electricity needs with the rest generated by hydro-electric power. An expansion of hydro-electric power has thus far been out of the question as parliament has decided not to dam any more rivers.
